We should have cut our losses eight months earlier.
Somebody could have escalated it, and nobody did.
The margin must have been wrong from the start.
By month eight it was a sunk cost, and we kept paying for it.

Before anybody speaks, let me tell you what I am not interested in this morning, which is who was to blame. Assume everybody in the case is competent and acting in good faith, because in my experience they usually are. The question I want is different. At what point had the decision already been taken, even though nobody in the room had said so yet? Now, a warning about a phrase I hear in every one of these discussions. They should have known. It is almost always the weakest sentence said in this room, because the information nearly always was there, in the building, on somebody's desk, in month two. So the real question is not whether they knew. It is why nobody acted on what they knew. By the end of the hour I want each of you to be able to name the exact moment when cutting their losses was still cheap, and to tell me what would have had to be true for somebody to do it.

The first red flag was a supplier who asked for payment in advance in month two, and I want to be honest about how we handled it: we treated it as a problem with that supplier. We did not read it as information about the project, and it was. That is the whole case, really. The part I still think about is month eight. By then the money was gone. It could not come back, it was not going to come back, and we kept making decisions as though it might, which cost us another four months on top of the eight. That is the definition of a sunk cost and I could have told you the definition at the time. Knowing the definition and behaving as if you know it are two different skills. What we do now is unglamorous. There is a post-mortem on every project, and the last question on the sheet is the one we used to leave blank: what we would do differently, written in full sentences, by the person who took the decision.
If we had seen the red flag, we would have stopped in April.
If the contingency had been bigger, the delay would not have mattered.
We should have cut our losses eight months earlier.
Somebody could have escalated it, and nobody did.
The margin must have been wrong from the start.
With a bigger contingency it might have gone the other way.
By month eight it was a sunk cost, and we kept paying for it.
